passage: People think caring for a parent is only about love. It's also about schedules. My father got Parkinson's when I was twenty-four. Suddenly I was juggling my IT job, his doctor visits and his medicines. My sister Gargi lived in Delhi and felt guilty all the time. At first I did everything and got angry with her quietly. Then we had a proper call. 'Karthik, give me jobs I can do from here,' she said. She took over the paperwork and insurance claims from Delhi, and sent money for a part-time helper. I handled the hospital visits. We made a shared calendar. Some nights I'm still exhausted and sad watching him struggle with buttons. But we're a team now, and I'm not doing it alone.

qa.q: What part of the care did Gargi take over?
qa.a: She took over the paperwork and insurance claims from Delhi and sent money for a part-time helper.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel before the proper call with Gargi?
qa.a: Karthik felt overwhelmed and quietly angry with Gargi for not sharing the load.

qa.q: What helped Karthik manage the father's care?
qa.a: Dividing tasks with Gargi, hiring a helper and keeping a shared calendar.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi living far away?
qa.a: She feels guilty about not being there, so doing the paperwork gives her a real way to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult managing time, money and feelings while caring for an ageing parent with their sister.

passage: I'm Vidya, and I live across the landing from Ujjwal. His grandmother moved in with him last spring after a fall. He's twenty-five, works shifts at a bank, and now I see him most mornings carrying her tea to the balcony before running for his bus. Sometimes I hear him on the phone with relatives, voice raised: 'I can't do everything.' Once I found him sitting on the stairs, just staring. I asked if he was okay, and he said he was fine, but he wasn't. I offered to check on her during the day. He hesitated, then accepted. He started paying a nurse for a few hours on weekends too. Now he leaves a note on her door with the day's plan.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal's grandmother move in with him?
qa.a: She moved in after a fall.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal sitting on the stairs, just staring, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was exhausted and overwhelmed, even though he said he was fine.

qa.q: How could neighbours support a young carer like Ujjwal?
qa.a: By offering specific help, like checking on the grandmother during the day, and not waiting to be asked.

qa.q: How does Vidya see Ujjwal's situation?
qa.a: Vidya sees that he's carrying a lot and pretending to be fine, and steps in with practical help.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young man struggle and adapt while caring for his grandmother.

passage:
First week: Ankita's mother started forgetting to take her medicines. Ankita moved back from the hostel and slept on the living room sofa. She missed two work deadlines and snapped at her brother Saurabh on the phone.

A month later: The doctor suggested memory checks. Ankita and Saurabh sat down with a list: who pays for what, who visits when, and what Ma could still do herself. Saurabh couldn't come often, so he took over the bills. Ankita cried for a while after that call, though she felt steadier too.

Three months later: Ankita had a pill box on the table and an alarm on Ma's phone. She had joined a carers' support group that met on Sundays. Ma still forgot things. But Ankita was sleeping again.

qa.q: Where did Ankita sleep after moving back?
qa.a: She slept on the living room sofa.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling in the first week, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and stressed; she missed deadlines and snapped at Saurabh.

qa.q: What helped Ankita most over the three months?
qa.a: Sharing tasks with Saurabh, simple routines like a pill box and alarm, and joining a carers' support group.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt living far away?
qa.a: He may have felt guilty for not being there, and taking on the bills let him help in a real way.

grounding: Shows a young woman, over months, managing time, money and emotions while caring for her ageing mother.

passage: Kishore puttar, sit with your Gurleen Aunty. You look like I did at twenty-five. My mother-in-law had a stroke the year after my wedding, and suddenly I was the one bathing her, feeding her, running to the chemist between my school job and home. I loved her, but some nights I sat in the bathroom and wanted to scream. Then I felt guilty for wanting to. What saved me was not strength. It was a family meeting. I made a list of every task and every cost and put it in front of my husband and his two brothers. They were shocked. One paid for a day attendant; the other came every Sunday so I could rest. Her doctor also told us about a caregivers' group that met in the gurudwara hall. Those women understood without my explaining. You can't carry Bapuji alone either, puttar. Make your list.

qa.q: What happened to Gurleen's mother-in-law the year after her wedding?
qa.a: She had a stroke.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Gurleen have on hard nights?
qa.a: She loved her mother-in-law but felt like screaming, and then felt guilty for wanting to.

qa.q: What helped Gurleen share the load?
qa.a: A written list of every task and cost shown at a family meeting, which brought paid help and Sunday rest, plus a caregivers' group.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's husband and his brothers have felt seeing the list?
qa.a: Shocked, realising how much she had been carrying without them noticing.

grounding: An elder recalls managing the time, money and feelings of caring for an ailing relative by sharing the load.

passage: The day attendant didn't come, the monsoon had knocked out the lift, and Himani had a client call at eleven. Her father, whose memory had been slipping for two years, kept asking where her mother was; she had died three years ago. Each time Himani answered gently, 'She's not here, Papa. I'm here.' At 10:50 she called her sister Pallavi in Bhopal. 'I can't do this call and watch him.' Pallavi, who usually sent money rather than time, said, 'Put me on video with him. I'll talk to him for an hour.' Papa loved it. Himani took the call from the balcony, hair unwashed, voice steady. Afterwards she sat on the floor and cried a little, mostly from tiredness. That evening the sisters made a plan: Pallavi would take two video hours a week and visit every month, and they would look for a backup attendant.

qa.q: What time was Himani's client call?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: How did Himani feel after the call, and why?
qa.a: She sat on the floor and cried a little, mostly from exhaustion after juggling work and her father's care alone.

qa.q: What did the sisters change so that care is shared more fairly?
qa.a: Pallavi will give two video hours a week and visit every month, and they will look for a backup attendant.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's role have felt different after that day?
qa.a: She moved from sending money to giving time, which may have made her feel closer to her father and sister.

grounding: Shows a young woman caring for her ageing father under pressure and sharing the load with her sister.

passage: By the third time her father left the gas on, Gurpreet stopped pretending it was fine. She worked in Gurgaon, and her father, retired and widowed, lived with her in their Janakpuri flat. His memory had been slipping for a year. She worked nine to six, cooked at night, and woke at 3 a.m. to check on him. Her sister Sarika, in Toronto, sent money and advice in equal amounts: "You should take him to the doctor." "I did," Gurpreet typed, too sharply. After that she sat down and made a list: what she could do, what she couldn't, what would cost money. She had a gas shut-off valve fitted, asked the aunty next door to look in at lunch, and visited a day centre for elders two streets away. The first day her father went, he came home talking about a carrom game. That night Gurpreet slept through for the first time in months.

qa.q: Where does Gurpreet's sister Sarika live?
qa.a: In Toronto.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet typing 'I did' too sharply suggest?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt exhausted and resentful, carrying the daily care while getting advice from far away.

qa.q: Which of Gurpreet's steps made the care more sustainable?
qa.a: Listing what she could and couldn't do, fitting a gas valve, arranging a neighbour's lunchtime check and finding a day centre, so she wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might Sarika feel sending money from far away?
qa.a: Sarika probably feels guilty and worried at being so far, which may come out as advice that sounds like blame.

grounding: A young woman in Delhi caring for her ageing father alone organises practical help and support to make it sustainable.

passage:
"I can't do another night," Hansa whispered in the corridor. "Mummyji called for water six times."
Sangeeta, her sister-in-law, leaned against the wall. "I know. I heard. I thought you wanted to do it all."
"I thought I had to. You work, and she's my husband's mother."
"She's my husband's mother too." Sangeeta rubbed her eyes. "Why didn't you ask?"
"Because everyone would say I'm not managing."
"You're not managing. Neither am I. Nobody could."
Hansa laughed, close to tears. "So what do we do?"
"A rota. You Monday, Wednesday, Friday nights. Me Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday. Sunday, the brothers."
"The brothers?" Hansa's eyebrows shot up. "Both of them?"
"They're her sons. They can hold a glass of water."
"And the physiotherapy bills?"
"All four of us sit down on Sunday and split them properly. No more one person paying and sulking."
Hansa hugged her, hard.

qa.q: How many times did Mummyji call for water?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What was Hansa worried about that stopped her asking for help?
qa.a: Hansa was afraid everyone would judge her as not managing, so she felt she had to do it all alone.

qa.q: What makes Sangeeta's plan fairer and more sustainable?
qa.a: A night rota that includes the brothers, and a Sunday talk to split the physiotherapy bills openly, so no one carries it alone.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see the situation?
qa.a: Sangeeta is exhausted too and sees that nobody could manage alone, so she wants the care shared, including by the sons.

grounding: Two sisters-in-law caring for an ageing mother-in-law agree to share nights, costs and the sons' role fairly.

passage: The year Nanaji moved in with us, I, Urmila, learned how many kinds of tired there are. He was eighty-four, proud and unsteady on his feet. I worked from home, so it became "natural" that I handled his medicines, his doctor visits and both his falls. My brother Chaitanya lived across the city and visited on Sundays with sweets. I loved Nanaji. I also started to resent everyone, including him, and then felt terrible about it. One night I snapped at him over his slippers, and he looked at me like a scolded child. I cried on the stairs. The next morning I called Chaitanya and said plainly, "I can't do this alone." He was quiet, then said, "I didn't know it was this much." Now he does Wednesday evenings and the doctor visits, and we found a caregiver for three mornings a week. I still get tired. But I don't snap, and Nanaji has started telling me stories again.

qa.q: How old was Nanaji when he moved in?
qa.a: Eighty-four.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling after snapping at Nanaji over his slippers?
qa.a: Urmila felt guilty and heartbroken, crying on the stairs after seeing his hurt face.

qa.q: What change made the caring bearable?
qa.a: Telling Chaitanya plainly that it was too much, which led to his Wednesday evenings and doctor visits, plus a paid caregiver three mornings a week.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have felt hearing 'I can't do this alone'?
qa.a: Chaitanya was probably surprised and guilty, not having realised how much it was, and moved to help more.

grounding: A young adult looks back on caring for an elderly grandfather, the resentment it brought, and sharing the load with a sibling.

passage:
Day-care centre note, Friday.

Sangeeta brings her father in at 8.40 every morning on her way to work and collects him at 6.30. Today she arrived late, apologising to everyone, her dupatta half off one shoulder. He had wandered out of the flat at 5 a.m. and a neighbour had walked him home.

She told me she has been sleeping about four hours and snapping at her son. "I love Papa," she said. "But some days I'm so angry, and then I feel terrible for being angry."

I told her both feelings are common for carers. We made a small plan: her brother in Nagpur will cover two weekend days a month, and I gave her the number of the carers' support group that meets on Thursday evenings here. I also asked her to talk to her father's doctor about the night wandering.

She wrote the list on her palm. I will check in with her on Monday.

— Zeenat, centre coordinator

qa.q: What time does Sangeeta collect her father?
qa.a: She collects him at 6.30.

qa.q: How is Sangeeta feeling about caring for her father?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels exhausted, sometimes angry, and then guilty for being angry, even though she loves him.

qa.q: What small steps did Zeenat help Sangeeta plan?
qa.a: Her brother will cover two weekend days a month, she will try the carers' support group, and she will talk to her father's doctor about the night wandering.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's son be affected by her exhaustion?
qa.a: He is being snapped at more often, so he may feel hurt or confused, and he would benefit from his mother getting more rest and support.

grounding: A day-care coordinator notes a young woman struggling with time and emotions while caring for her father, and helps her plan support.

passage:
Thursday, Darjeeling

Ama-la had a good morning. She remembered the neighbour's name and asked for her tea with extra salt, the old way. I logged into work at nine from the kitchen table so I could hear her if she called.

Afternoon was harder. She thought I was my mother and kept asking when Papa was coming home. I had a client call. I muted myself twice to answer her gently. By six my shoulders were up by my ears.

Video call with Indu in Dubai tonight. I finally said it: "I can't do all of this alone and keep my job." She went quiet, then said, "What can I take from here?"

We decided: Indu manages her medicine orders and the doctor's appointments online. She'll also pay for a helper three mornings a week, and I'll handle the rest of the bills. Saying it out loud was the hardest part.

Tenzin

qa.q: What did Ama-la ask for with her tea?
qa.a: She asked for her tea with extra salt, the old way.

qa.q: How was Tenzin feeling by six in the evening?
qa.a: Tenzin felt tense and stretched thin, with shoulders up by the ears after juggling work and gently answering Ama-la.

qa.q: What made the call with Indu useful?
qa.a: Tenzin named the problem honestly, and they split concrete tasks, so the care no longer rested on one person.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about hearing Tenzin's words from far away?
qa.a: Indu might feel guilty for being far away, but also relieved to be asked for real tasks she can do from Dubai.

grounding: A young adult caring for a grandmother while working admits the strain and shares time, money and tasks with a sibling abroad.

passage:
Jaya, twenty-five, had moved back to her small town in Karnataka when her father's memory began to fail. She worked remotely for a firm in Bengaluru, which helped. But between his doctor visits, cooking, and his confused nights, she was always tired.
Her brother Harsha, in Mumbai, sent money every month and felt that was enough. One Sunday, on a video call, Jaya finally cried. "I need you here, not just your money."
Harsha was quiet. Then he said, "Tell me what would help."
They made a plan: Harsha would come home one week every two months so Jaya could rest; he'd handle all the paperwork and insurance from Mumbai; they'd ask the local health worker about a day-care centre for elders twice a week.
Jaya still had hard days. But the next month, she slept through two nights while Harsha sat up with their father.

qa.q: How often would Harsha come home, according to the plan?
qa.a: One week every two months.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she cried on the video call?
qa.a: Jaya felt exhausted and alone, carrying their father's care while her brother only sent money.

qa.q: What made their plan fairer for both siblings?
qa.a: It shared time as well as money, gave Harsha remote tasks he could do from Mumbai, and added outside help from a day-care centre.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt hearing Jaya cry?
qa.a: Harsha probably felt shocked and guilty, realising money alone hadn't lightened her load.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult caring for an ageing parent and renegotiating time, money and emotional load with a sibling.

passage:
In a small town outside Kyoto, Hana and her younger brother Hiroshi took turns staying with their grandmother, who had started forgetting things: the stove, the day, sometimes their names.
Hana was twenty-four, working at a bakery. Hiroshi was at university. Their parents worked long hours in Osaka.
One night Hana found her grandmother trying to leave the house at 2 a.m. "I'm going to the station to meet your grandfather," she said. He had died ten years ago.
Hana felt her chest tighten. She didn't argue. She walked with her grandmother to the garden and back, talking about the station, until she was calm enough to sleep.
The next morning, Hana called a family meeting on video. She said, "I love her, and I can't do nights alone anymore." They agreed to ask the town's elder-care office for a visiting nurse and a door alarm, and Hiroshi would take weekend nights.

qa.q: Where did Hana's grandmother say she was going at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: To the station to meet their grandfather.

qa.q: How did Hana feel when her grandmother said she was meeting their grandfather?
qa.a: Hana felt heartbroken and tense, her chest tightening, because he had died ten years ago.

qa.q: Which of Hana's choices helped, both that night and after?
qa.a: She stayed calm and walked with her grandmother instead of arguing, then asked the family for shared help and outside support.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi feel taking weekend nights?
qa.a: Hiroshi might feel nervous about handling the nights but glad to share the load with his sister.

grounding: Shows a young adult managing emotions and time while caring for a grandmother with memory problems, and seeking help.

passage:
In the hospital's family room, Nazia sat with the social worker, Chinmay, after her mother's second fall in a month. Her mother was seventy-eight and wanted to go home. Nazia, twenty-six, worked full time and lived alone with her.
"I'm scared she'll fall again when I'm at work," Nazia said. "And I feel guilty even thinking about a care home."
Chinmay nodded. "Both feelings make sense. Let's look at the choices, not just one."
He explained options: a trained home attendant for daytime, grab bars and a ramp at home, a community day-care centre, and her mother's pension and insurance that might cover some of it. He also suggested a caregivers' support group on Thursdays.
Nazia wrote everything down. Her mother, when asked, chose the attendant and the day-care centre twice a week.
Nazia left the hospital still tired, but no longer feeling she had to choose between her job and her mother.

qa.q: How many times had Nazia's mother fallen in a month?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling about her mother's care?
qa.a: Nazia felt scared about another fall and guilty for even thinking about a care home.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do that helped Nazia make a decision?
qa.a: He accepted her feelings, laid out several options with possible support, and suggested a caregivers' group.

qa.q: How might Nazia's mother feel being asked to choose?
qa.a: Her mother probably felt respected and less like a burden, having a say in her own care.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult balancing work, guilt and practical options while arranging care for an ageing parent.

passage:
Vaibhav,
I'm writing instead of calling because I lose my temper on calls, and I don't want to this time.
Baba fell again on Tuesday. Not badly, a bruised wrist, but he was on the bathroom floor for twenty minutes before the neighbour heard him. I've been going over every evening after work, and I'm running on four hours of sleep. I snapped at him yesterday for forgetting his tablets, then sat in the car and cried.
I love him. I also can't do this alone anymore.
Here's what I'm asking. Can you cover half the cost of a daytime attendant? I've found an agency the doctor recommended. Can you video-call him every Sunday so he has something to look forward to? And when you visit in December, can you take the week so I can rest?
I'm not angry at you. I'm tired.
Kiran

qa.q: How long was Baba on the bathroom floor before the neighbour heard him?
qa.a: He was on the floor for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Kiran feeling, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kiran feels exhausted and guilty, running on four hours of sleep, snapping at Baba and then crying in the car, while still loving him.

qa.q: Why is Kiran's letter a good way to share the load?
qa.a: It explains calmly, avoids blame, and asks for three concrete things: half the attendant's cost, Sunday calls, and a week of rest in December.

qa.q: What might it be like for Baba to be cared for this way?
qa.a: Baba might feel embarrassed about falling and forgetting, and comforted by Sunday calls to look forward to.

grounding: Shows a young adult balancing time, money and emotions in caring for an ageing parent and asking a sibling to share it.
